newsitem.title: USA: American pilots remain opposed to binding arbitration.
newsitem.headline: American pilots remain opposed to binding arbitration.

text.p: The American Airlines pilots' union said on Thursday it would welcome President Bill Clinton's help in trying to avert a pending strike, although the pilots remained opposed to binding arbitration.

Wally Pitts, a spokesman for the Allied Pilots Association, said his union preferred to settle the dispute with American without government intervention, "but if the president does decide to get involved, we're good citizens and will follow his lead." However, referring to binding arbitration, he said "I seriously doubt we could accept that."
Robert Crandall, chairman of AMR Corp., American's parent, earlier had reiterated his support for binding arbitration to settle the airline's two-year-old dispute with its pilots.
The comments by Pitts and Crandall came with less than 36 hours remaining before the pilots' scheduled midnight Friday strike against American.
Clinton said Wednesday that he was watching the deliberations closely and urged the sides to use a mediation process to resolve their dispute, which he said had "huge implications" for the country.

He has the authority to convene an emergency board, which once formed would prevent a strike at least tempoprarily, while it tries to formulate a contract agreeable to both parties. The parties would be refrained from striking for 30 days while they decided whether or not to accept the panel's compromise contract.
The union offer would fly the new jet under the American Airlines banner, but pay the pilots less than those flying the big jets.
American Airlines spokesman Al Comeaux said the carrier was not rejecting the idea because "it was not a proposal," adding "it was a bunch of verbiage on paper."
He said "we've asked for details. What we've actually asked for is a proposal."
Commenting later, a union spokesman said the union would detail the proposal later today and "we hope they give it serious consideration."
The spokesman added that the plan would enable American to fly smaller jets with APA pilots, yet remain competitive with other major airlines providing low-cost regional services.
